messages.subject: Re: CODEX copy number neutral events
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tenghui,

Yes, the default output of CODEX is tab-delimited txt files that include whether a cnv region is a deletion or a duplication and the specific copy number for the region. Note that there are two ‘modes’ in CODEX: the ‘integer’ mode returns integer copy numbers and therefore all regions that are not called to harbor CNV have copy number = 2; the ‘fraction’ mode returns fractional copy numbers (this mode is useful for calling CNVs in tumor samples due to cancer heterogeneity and normal cell contamination etc). For the fractional mode, the output txt files include CNV events with continuous copy numbers and thus a thresholding procedure needs to be adopted. Each CNV regions come with a copy number, even for copy number neutral regions.

Hope this answers your question! I am cc’ing our user group in case other users have similar questions.

Cheers,
Yuchao

messages.subject: Re: Codex
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fatima,

Thanks for being patient and sorry for replying a bit late -- I’ve been traveling for the past few days. For analyzing tumor samples, especially tumors with large and frequent chromosomal aberrations (e.g. breast/ovarian cancer), it’s better if normal samples are included as input. The normal_index specifies which samples are normals. CODEX uses a multi-sample normalization procedure (rather than directly compares tumor against normal as it is by no means adequate to capture all the biases and artifact). More specifically, the exon specific latent factors and the beta term are estimated using the normal samples only (this is why the index of the normals needs to be specified); the sample specific latent factors are then estimated using regression. The current version of CODEX doesn’t utilize the paired information but from our collaboration (WES 38 paired tumor normal breast/ovarian cancer) we show that it works well to detect all expected somatic CNVs, some spanning the entire chromosomal arms. We, however, have a version of segmentation that uses the pair information (intuitively, by comparing the ratio of normalized versus original read depth in tumor versus normal). If you are interested, I can share that with you.

With this said, CODEX can be used to detect germline CNVs in normal samples only and tumor samples with few structural variants (e.g. pediatric cancer). In this case, parameters are estimated using all exons across all samples.

Another thing you need to be careful with is that if your samples come with hight proportions of normal cell contamination or sub-clonal events, use the ‘fractional’ model instead of the ‘integer’ one.

Hope this helps and let me know if you have any further questions,
Yuchao
